notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0022.tlg001.1st1K-gr: θιβρήν (line 35), rendered ‘hot’, is obscure. βλῆτρον (39) is an unidentified plant. The stone of Gagai (37) is jet. ἀσκελές (42), ‘hard’, may mean ‘dry’. ἀμολγοί (49), ‘milkers’, are herdsmen.

nodes.text: is dim in his eyes; but the luxuriant shoot of fennel,
once grazed, makes him swift and clear-sighted.
You will drive off the hot, harmful bane of snakes
by burning the many-pointed antler of a stag,
or at other times kindling the dry stone of Gagai,
which not even the onset of strong fire overcomes;
and throw into the fire the leafage of the much-cleft bletron;
or take the fire-hot root that bears cachrys,
mixed with an equal weight of cress; and mix in the strong-smelling
fresh, hard horn of a roe, setting it in the scale-pan,
and of heavy-scented nigella, at other times of sulphur,
at other times of bitumen, bringing a share of equal weight;
or you might set the Thracian stone ablaze in fire,
which, when wetted with water, blazes, but quenches its gleam
when it scents even a little oil sprinkled on it.
This the herdsmen bring from the Thracian river
which they call Pontus; there the Thracian milkers,
